title: Sowing coriander microgreens
subtitle: How to prepare and sow coriander seed — including the hull-cracking step
excerpt: Coriander seed requires an overnight soak and a light hull-cracking before sowing. The outer corky hull contains two seeds and slows germination significantly if left intact. Preparing the seed the night before sowing makes a measurable difference to germination rates.
sourceNotes: UMass Extension microgreens guides (open-access). Cornell Cooperative Extension indoor growing material. Standard microgreen-growing practice synthesised from extension service material.

glossaryTerms.definition: Rinsing seed before sowing to remove dust, seed-treatment residues, and surface sugars that can encourage mould on microgreen trays. For coriander, rinsing after soaking and cracking removes fragments of the outer hull and surface sugars before sowing.

The period immediately after sowing when a second tray is stacked on top, blocking light from the sown tray. In darkness, germinating seeds direct energy into pushing the shoot upward. For coriander, the blackout phase runs four to five days due to the slower germination of this crop.

content.text: Coriander seed is unusual in the microgreen range: what looks like a single round seed is actually a corky outer hull containing two seeds. This hull is slow to absorb water and slows germination considerably if left intact. Cracking the hull before sowing gives the inner seeds direct contact with moisture.

One 25 cm × 25 cm growing tray. A second tray for the blackout cover. Seed compost. Coriander seed: 15 to 20 g per tray. A bowl for soaking. Two sheets of paper and a rolling pin or heavy flat object for cracking the hull. A sieve for rinsing after cracking.

Step 1: soak the seed. Place coriander seed in a bowl of room-temperature water and soak for 8 to 12 hours. The outer hull softens slightly and the seeds swell. The soak water becomes cloudy from surface material released by the hull.

Step 2: drain and crack. Drain the soaked seeds. Spread them between two sheets of paper (a paper bag works well). Roll over the seeds firmly once with a rolling pin or press with a flat heavy object. The aim is to crack the outer hull without splitting the inner seeds. The seeds will flatten slightly and the outer hull will split or loosen.
: after cracking, rinse the seeds through a fine sieve under cold running water to remove loose hull fragments and surface sugars.
Step 3: fill the tray with pre-dampened seed compost to within 1 cm of the rim and level the surface.

Step 4: scatter the cracked coriander seed at 15 to 20 g per tray. The seed is bulkier and less uniformly round after cracking; scatter from 15 cm above the tray in small quantities, distributing systematically. Press gently into contact with the medium.

: cover with a second tray and a light weight. Coriander germinates more slowly than brassicas; expect four to five days in the blackout. Check for upright shoots at 2 to 3 cm before removing the cover.

attrs.heading: Troubleshooting
attrs.intro: Common sowing-stage problems with coriander microgreens.

items.symptom: Very sparse germination even after cracking
items.cause: Old seed, insufficient hull cracking, or cold room.
items.fix: Use seed from the current growing season. Apply more pressure when cracking the hull; the outer layer should visibly split. Room temperature should be above 18°C.

items.symptom: Cracking splits too many seeds entirely
items.cause: Too much pressure applied during the cracking step.
items.fix: Use lighter pressure. The goal is to crack the outer hull only; the inner seed should remain mostly intact. Some damage to a few seeds is acceptable.

items.symptom: Mould appearing on the medium by day 3 of blackout
items.cause: Inadequate rinsing after cracking, leaving surface sugars on the seed.
items.fix: Rinse more thoroughly after cracking on the next attempt. Bottom-water only and maintain airflow.
